activities.anchor: government spending and taxation as an economic lever
activities.caption: automatic or discretionary?
activities.name: fpStabiliserSort

items.label: unemployment benefits rise as jobs disappear
parliament passes a new infrastructure programme
tax receipts fall when incomes fall
the government cuts VAT for one year
pension payments rise with the rules
a one-off stimulus cheque is legislated

config.why: Automatic stabilisers widen the deficit without a vote; discretionary policy is the part politicians argue about.

activities.caption: pair each lever with its example
activities.name: fpLeversMatch

config.prompt: Pair each fiscal lever with what it does:

pairs.right: build a bridge — buys output directly
a pension or benefit — redistributes without buying output
withdraw purchasing power; cutting them is a stimulus

config.why: Purchases enter G directly; transfers stimulate only when recipients spend them; taxes change the purchasing power left in private hands.

config.prompt: A £10bn programme is spent by households with MPC = 0.8. In the frictionless multiplier, what is the total rise in GDP?
config.why: Multiplier = 1/(1 − 0.8) = 5, so £10bn × 5 = £50bn. Leakages into taxes, imports and saving make the real figure smaller.
config.context: with MPC 0.6 the multiplier would be 2.5

activities.anchor: The debt ratio D (debt ÷ GDP) evolves by one inequality
activities.caption: mark the stabilising primary surplus
activities.name: fpDebtPlace

config.prompt: Debt is 100% of GDP, the interest rate is 5% and nominal growth is 3%. What primary surplus, as a share of GDP, stabilises the ratio? Place it.
config.why: (i − y) × D = (5% − 3%) × 100% = 2% of GDP. Without that surplus the ratio drifts up.

activities.caption: true or false — who bears the debt
activities.name: fpBurdenJudge

statements.s: If debt is held domestically, servicing it is largely a transfer from future taxpayers to future bondholders.
statements.why: The payment circulates within the country; the question becomes distributional rather than an international loss.

statements.s: If the debt is owed to ourselves, it has no economic costs at all.
statements.why: Incentive costs from the taxes that service it, the foreign-held share, and lost crisis room all survive the accounting.

statements.s: A heavily indebted country has less room to respond to the next crisis.
statements.why: Pre-existing debt constrains the fiscal response, as the 2010 eurozone members discovered.

statements.s: Bond interest flows disproportionately to wealthier savers.
statements.why: The servicing is financed by broader taxpayers and paid to bondholders, a quietly regressive transfer.

activities.anchor: The single biggest risk factor in public debt is the currency
activities.caption: own currency or foreign currency?
activities.name: fpCurrencyBranch

config.root: Two governments have debt at 150% of GDP. One borrows in its own currency; the other borrows in dollars. Trace the crisis menu.

start.text: Markets begin to doubt repayment. Which government faces genuine default risk?

choices.label: The dollar borrower — it cannot print dollars
choices.feedback: Yes — it must find dollars or restructure.

choices.label: The own-currency borrower — it must default
choices.feedback: It can always create the currency; the risk shifts to inflation.

choices.label: Both face identical risk
choices.feedback: The currency changes the menu completely.

right.text: The foreign-currency borrower can be forced into default: yields spike, refinancing closes, and the IMF arrives with conditions. The own-currency government's crisis mode is inflation, not bankruptcy.

own.text: An own-currency government cannot be forced into involuntary default — it can print. The cost is inflation, which taxes savers.

choices.label: Compare the two cases
choices.feedback: Foreign-currency debt risks default; own-currency debt risks inflation.

same.text: The currency is the biggest risk factor: own-currency debt risks inflation, foreign-currency debt risks default.

choices.label: Which is which?
choices.feedback: The dollar borrower faces the default wall.

config.why: Own-currency debt cannot force involuntary default — the escape valve is inflation; foreign-currency and shared-currency debt can force a restructuring.

activities.anchor: Because the slope is gradual, crises announce themselves
activities.caption: how a rollover crisis unfolds
activities.name: fpCrisisOrder

config.prompt: A rollover crisis unfolds — put the sequence in order:
items: Markets begin to doubt the government's ability to repay
New bond issues demand punitive yields
The interest bill eats a growing share of the budget
Refinancing becomes harder and the spiral turns self-fulfilling
config.why: The rollover squeeze is self-reinforcing: doubt raises yields, higher yields worsen the budget, and worse budgets confirm the doubt.

activities.caption: headline versus structural deficit — drag the divider
activities.name: fpDeficitCompare

config.prompt: Two ways to read a deficit — drag the divider:

before.label: headline deficit
before.text: the actual budget balance this year — widened automatically by recession

after.label: structural deficit
after.text: the balance after stripping out the cycle — the underlying policy stance

config.why: The cyclical part is the stabilisers doing their job; the structural part is the choice. Comparing budgets across years without that distinction misreads the stance.

activities.anchor: The austerity debate, in one paragraph
activities.caption: find the self-defeating arithmetic
activities.name: fpAusteritySpot

config.prompt: Find the line where the austerity arithmetic goes wrong:
lines: After 2010, eurozone governments cut spending to reassure bond markets.
The IMF assumed multipliers around 0.5, so the cuts would shrink GDP only modestly.
In the event, multipliers were much larger, so GDP fell further than predicted.
A smaller GDP mechanically lowers the debt ratio, so austerity worked as intended.
The lesson is that consolidation in a slump can be self-defeating.
config.correction: A smaller GDP raises the debt ratio, not lowers it — that is why the consolidation was self-defeating.
config.why: The denominator shrank, so the ratio the policy meant to cut rose.

config.text: Ricardian equivalence says today's deficit is tomorrow's %%0%%, so forward-looking households %%1%% the stimulus rather than spend it; empirically the effect is %%2%% because many households are liquidity-constrained.
config.hint: If the deficit is just deferred taxation, a perfectly forward-looking household saves the windfall.
